commits.summary: The default run builds Rust's tests in a lightly optimised profile and takes 3.4 minutes: the engine's own tests are several times faster for a build twice as long
commits.body: lib/Cargo.toml gains the profile test-fast (dev with its checks, opt-level 1, line tables only, the SAT solver at 3 as in dev), and test_costs.py run uses it for the default and unit tiers; the proof tier stays in release and plain cargo test stays dev, each in its own folder of target/. Measured on this machine on 2026-11-17, each binary alone: tests/alignment.rs 94 s as dev and 10 s in test-fast, summaries 13 s and 5 s, conformance 45 s and 36 s, application_core_joint 147 s and 123 s, integration and heap unchanged; the profile's first build 69 s, and a build after an edit in src/bmc/mod.rs 14 s where dev takes 7 s. The whole default run with it: 201 s, 49 of 49 passed, the Rust binaries 163 s of it (276 s and 230 s in the commit before). The job queued in the commit before, 20261117-003114, passed in 518 s on six CPUs without this profile, where the first job took 1170 s.

commits.summary: Example 290's results are stated at their exact scope, and VF-033 queues a stronger preservation claim and an audit of the observed initializers for a later run
commits.body: The user's decision on reviewing D005 (the watcher's acceptance of 290's claims in their place): keep the claims and their verdicts, say exactly what they cover, and queue the rest. 290's page and example.json notes now say that preservation is established for the count of matchers by type in the lone-DispatcherServlet configuration, not for the matchers themselves or what they match, and that fixed-security and preservation hold under the observation of library initializers on a JVM: two of them load resource bundles, so 'no input' is that observation's assumption until the state read is audited (points 1 and 2 of the outside expert's c3 review); the refutations replay on a JVM and do not rest on it. VF-033 (open) records both, with the chosen follow-up (restate preservation to compare each matcher's type, pattern, HTTP method and servlet path: a setup and about one proof cycle) and the one not chosen (compare matches(), which needs HandlerMappingIntrospector modelled). Verified: validate_example.py 290 passes.

commits.summary: What a default run left unread is a plain output file of the job, and its log says only how many paths
commits.body: The packed line (default tests: unread zlib:...) was opaque to the redaction scanner and raised a long-token warning in every transcript and log that showed it (finding fd843c30, after the merge of prove-setup). The step now writes verification/default-tests-unread.txt, the job's id and then one path a line, as a declared output: the pipeline applies it to the working copy when it collects a passed run and keeps a failed or late run's under the result's outputs/. default_tests.py reads a run's list from there (the kept copy first, else the file when its first line names the job), so the gate uses the list of the latest passed run and older runs cover by the fixed list alone; the file itself is on that list. The two runs already collected with a packed line no longer have a list. Checked with the suite's new tests (the step writes the file and prints a count; a run finds its list applied or kept) and test_costs.py run --changed: 14 of 14 passed.

commits.summary: Only one default test run runs at a time, and a job started again after a newer run finished is superseded
commits.body:
Two default-run jobs ran at once on 2026-11-17 (010456, and 005759 started a second time after it had passed): they share the warm cargo target directory and the tests' work folders under its tmp/, and eight Rust tests that pass alone failed in one run and passed on its retry, while the other's rerun failed. default_tests.py step now holds an exclusive lock (flock on ~/.cache/in-the-loop/default-tests.lock, beside the target directory) for the whole run and its bisect; a second step says it is waiting, waits, and asks the queue again once it has the lock.

Superseding looked only at jobs pending or running, and read a job's id only at the start of a status row. It now also counts a newer default run that has finished or been collected, so a passed job the runner starts again exits at once, finds the id anywhere in the row, and says in the log when the queue could not be read (it then runs, as before). Why the runner started a passed job again is not found: that is in pipeline.py's collecting, not here. Checked with three new tests (a held lock makes a second step wait and re-ask; a newer collected run; an unreadable queue), the 13 Python test files test_costs.py run --changed chose, and tests/tiers.rs.

commits.summary: /run-brief: an open Opus session becomes the watcher or takes a run over, and the preflight sees a loop at work and loops sharing a session
commits.body:
The user wants to start a brief's run from a session that is already open, which then is the watcher. The skill says so: any Opus 5.5 session of the default workspace can be asked in words, the run's state is all in files, and a new section, A run under way, has the watcher read brief_run.py status first and either go straight to waiting (a run it takes over), continue an interrupted run, or start a new one.

Two gaps in the preflight, found by checking it against the proof run under way: feature-loop.sh runs from a private copy of itself, so looking for prove-loop.sh by name missed a running proof loop, and the preflight now blocks on any feature loop at work in the default workspace; and a brief without a session setting falls back on the loops' one default session, so each brief of the run must name a session and no two the same.

Verified by test_brief_run.py, 26 tests, and the cost-tier lint. The whole default run was not repeated: it passed 49 of 49 on the commit before, and only brief_run.py, its tests, the skill and the README changed since.
